title: Write a Design Document: A Notification System
intro: This one has no walkthrough: design it yourself from the pieces in the earlier tutorials. The brief: a service that other teams call to send notifications by email, SMS, and mobile push. 50 million notifications a day, with bursts when marketing sends a campaign. A password-reset email must arrive within seconds even during a campaign. No user should get the same notification twice, and users can opt out per channel.

steps.prompt:
Write design-notification-system.md with a '# Design: ...' title and these level-2 sections, in this order, none empty:
## Requirements
## Estimates           (must convert 50 million a day into a per-second rate)
## API                 (must include POST /notifications and an idempotency key)
## Architecture        (must use a queue between the API and the senders, with separate workers per channel)
## Prioritisation      (how a password reset gets ahead of a marketing campaign: separate queues by priority)
## Reliability         (must cover retries with backoff, a dead-letter queue, and how duplicates are prevented)
## User preferences    (opt-outs, and rate limits per user)
## Failure modes       (what happens when a provider, such as the SMS vendor, is down)
## Trade-offs
steps.hint: Use exactly those headings. 50,000,000 / 86,400 is about 580 per second on average; say what a campaign burst could be. The key ideas: the API only validates and enqueues; a queue per priority so transactional messages never wait behind bulk; workers per channel; an idempotency key from the caller, recorded so a retried request sends nothing new; retries with exponential backoff, then a dead-letter queue; check opt-outs before sending; a second provider, or a queue that holds messages, when a provider is down.
steps.solution:
# Design: Notification System

## Requirements

Functional: other services request notifications by email, SMS, or mobile push; users can opt out per channel.
Non-functional: 50 million a day with campaign bursts; transactional messages such as password resets delivered within seconds; no duplicate sends; delivery status visible to callers.

## Estimates

50 million a day is about 580/s on average. A marketing campaign to 10 million users adds a burst of thousands per second for an hour.
Status records at about 500 bytes each are 25 GB a day; keep 90 days.

## API

POST /notifications with the recipient, channel, template, parameters, priority, and an idempotency key chosen by the caller.
The API validates, records the request, enqueues it, and returns 202 with a notification id.
GET /notifications/{id} returns its status.

## Architecture

The API writes each request to a queue; it never calls a provider itself.
Separate worker pools per channel (email, SMS, push) consume from the queue, render the template, and call the provider.
A status store records each attempt and the final outcome.

## Prioritisation

There are separate queues by priority: transactional (password resets, receipts) and bulk (campaigns).
Transactional queues have dedicated workers, so a campaign of millions cannot delay them.
Bulk sending is rate-limited to what the providers allow.

## Reliability

A failed send is retried with exponential backoff and jitter; after the last attempt it goes to a dead-letter queue and alerts.
Duplicates are prevented by the idempotency key: the request is recorded with a unique constraint on the key, so a retried request returns the original result and sends nothing new.
Workers record a send before acknowledging the message, and check that record before sending.

## User preferences

A preferences service holds each user's opt-out per channel and category; workers check it immediately before sending, since a preference can change after a message was queued.
A per-user rate limit caps how many notifications one person receives per hour.

## Failure modes

If a provider such as the SMS vendor is down, its workers stop consuming and the messages wait in the queue; transactional SMS fails over to a second provider.
If the queue backs up, bulk messages past their useful lifetime are dropped by a time-to-live; transactional ones are not.
If the preferences service is unavailable, bulk sending pauses and transactional sending continues.

## Trade-offs

A queue makes sending asynchronous: callers get an id, not a delivery guarantee, and must check status.
At-least-once processing with idempotency keys is simpler and safer than attempting exactly-once.
Separate priority queues cost more idle capacity and guarantee that urgent messages are never stuck behind bulk ones.
steps.explanation: A design in which a campaign can't delay a password reset, a retry can't send twice, and a provider outage delays messages instead of losing them.
steps.why: This design reuses nearly every idea in the category, which is what real design work is. The queue decouples callers from slow, unreliable providers (systemdesign-tutorial-007). Separate queues by priority are the answer to 'one workload starving another', the same idea as reserved concurrency and bounded queues elsewhere in this game. The idempotency key is systemdesign-incident-003's lesson. Retries with backoff and a dead-letter queue come from the messaging category. Checking opt-outs at send time, not at enqueue time, is the kind of detail a review looks for: the state can change while the message waits. As before, the checker confirms the structure and key terms only. The questions a reviewer would ask next: how do you stop one misbehaving caller flooding the transactional queue, and what does the status of a notification mean when the provider accepted it and the user's phone was off?
